name: Positive illusions
statement: Taylor and Brown argued that overly positive views of the self, of one's control and of one's future are normal and promote mental health.
meaning: Positive illusions is an umbrella term for three patterns treated as one syndrome: unrealistically positive self-evaluation, exaggerated perceptions of control, and unrealistic optimism. Whether each pattern exists is the subject of the entries on illusory superiority, illusion of control and optimism bias. This entry is about the further claim Taylor and Brown attached to them in 1988. That claim has two halves. The prevalence half says most healthy adults hold these beliefs, so accuracy cannot be a requirement of mental health. The adaptiveness half says the beliefs cause happiness, the ability to care about others and the capacity for productive work, rather than following from them. Only the second half is contested, and it is the half that made the paper famous.

origin.who: Shelley E. Taylor and Jonathon D. Brown
origin.note: The paper reviews existing work rather than reporting a study. Its target is the position, which it attributes to Jahoda and to Jourard and Landsman, that contact with reality is a criterion of mental health.

evidence: Taylor and Brown ran no experiment. They assembled evidence that most people hold overly positive self-evaluations, exaggerated perceptions of control or mastery, and unrealistic optimism, then asked whether those beliefs meet the criteria clinical writers use for mental health. Their method for the second step is stated openly. They take the criteria from Jahoda's 1958 review and from Jourard and Landsman, remove accurate self-perception from the list on the grounds that it is the thing in dispute, and keep three of what remains: happiness or contentment, the ability to care for and about others, and the capacity for creative and productive work. They then review studies linking each illusion to each criterion. Their own summary concedes that the research does not systematically address every illusion against every criterion and calls the evidence suggestive. Colvin and Block replied in 1994 that the logic and the studies failed to substantiate the thesis. The closing line of their abstract says the thesis remains unproven, but their own conclusion goes further, calling it unproven at best and possibly seriously wrong in many circumstances. Taylor and Brown's reply in the same issue narrowed the claim in three ways. The benefits are asserted for moderate illusion only, extreme illusion may be maladaptive, and illusion is not claimed to be necessary for mental health.

examples.tag: The student who expects the top band
examples.text: A first-year rates their ability above most of the cohort, expects to finish near the top and works with confidence. Most of a cohort cannot be above most of it. Whether holding the belief helps is a separate question from whether it is accurate.

examples.tag: Our marriage is not the statistic
examples.text: A couple can quote the divorce rate and put their own chance well below it, and they plan on that basis. The estimate of the world is fine and the estimate of themselves is not, and the two sit together without friction.

Someone convalescing believes their own discipline about exercise is driving the recovery more than the medicine or the passage of time. The belief keeps them at the exercises, which is the claim about usefulness rather than the claim about truth.

replication.headline: A meta-analysis of 299 samples puts self-enhancement at r = 0.18 with self-reported adjustment and at r = -0.01 with how favourably informants judge the person overall.
replication.detail: Dufner, Gebauer, Sedikides and Denissen pooled 299 samples and 126,916 people in 2019. They take the definition from Taylor and Brown among others, then pool four families of measure: criterion discrepancy, self-enhancing social comparison, grandiose narcissism and socially desirable responding. They say themselves that the last three are not pure measures of self-enhancement. The gold-standard subset behaves like the rest, r = .20, 95% CI [.16, .23], k = 25, N = 5,589. For self-reported personal adjustment the effect was r = .18, 95% CI [.17, .20], from 237 studies and 117,141 people. Self-enhancers reporting that they are happy is close to circular, so the informant analyses matter more. Informants rated self-enhancers as better adjusted, r = .12, 95% CI [.08, .17], k = 29, N = 4,760, and the six studies using trained mental health experts as raters gave r = .25, 95% CI [.17, .32], N = 681. Ten longitudinal studies covering 1,432 people found self-enhancement predicted later adjustment with concurrent correlations controlled, beta = .14, 95% CI [.09, .19]. Trim and fill filled 44 studies and moved the overall estimate to .14, 95% CI [.12, .16]. Under adverse life circumstances the effect was r = .16, 95% CI [.10, .21], k = 19, N = 3,440, which is the condition Taylor and Brown's cancer-patient work emphasised. The interpersonal side is not a flat null but a split. Self-enhancement was unrelated to how favourably informants judged the person overall, r = -.01, 95% CI [-.06, .04], k = 55, N = 11,794, and r = .02, 95% CI [-.03, .07], k = 50, N = 10,615, once eight studies with a biased design were dropped. Split by acquaintance, it predicted approval from strangers, r = .11, 95% CI [.03, .18], k = 22, N = 3,633, and nothing from people who had met the target before, r = -.04, 95% CI [-.09, .01], k = 30, N = 7,201. By content the results diverge. Agentic self-enhancers won an agentic reputation, r = .21, 95% CI [.14, .29], k = 17, N = 3,124, and lost a communal one, r = -.10, 95% CI [-.14, -.05], k = 22, N = 6,226. Communal self-enhancers won a communal reputation, r = .12, 95% CI [.07, .18], k = 9, N = 2,064. The authors call the interpersonal side a mixed blessing rather than nothing at all.

study.cite: Dufner, M., Gebauer, J. E., Sedikides, C., & Denissen, J. J. A. (2019). Self-enhancement and psychological adjustment: A meta-analytic review. Personality and Social Psychology Review, 23(1), 48-72.

limits: The measure is the weak point of the whole literature. Zuckerman and Knee pointed out in 1996 that a self-enhancement score built by subtracting others' ratings from self-ratings adds no variance once both ratings are in the model, so the index cannot show what self-enhancement does, and they proposed testing the interaction instead. Dufner and colleagues found that the objection has teeth in one specific case. Where self-enhancement was computed by subtracting informant ratings from self-ratings and correlated with an outcome also rated by informants, the result was negative for interpersonal adjustment, r = -.22, 95% CI [-.40, -.03], k = 8, N = 2,054, and for personal adjustment, r = -.17, 95% CI [-.26, -.08], k = 3, N = 437. That is the design of the best-known critical studies. Humberg and nine co-authors ran the sharpest test of the graded claim in 2019, using response surface analysis on five samples totalling 2,823 people and two ability domains, reasoning and vocabulary. Most adjustment indicators were best predicted by how positive the self-view was, and the evidence went against both the self-knowledge hypothesis and the optimal margin hypothesis. Two cautions belong with that result. Humberg's paper credits the optimal margin idea to Baumeister rather than to Taylor and Brown, and it does report specific self-enhancement effects, running in both directions across the two domains. One line of the argument has been tested on the body rather than on questionnaires. Taylor, Lerner, Sherman, Sage and McDowell put self-enhancers through a laboratory stress challenge in 2003 and found lower cardiovascular responses, faster recovery and lower baseline cortisol, against the view that self-enhancement is defensive neuroticism carrying a physiological cost. Dufner's domain-general interpersonal measure records overall favourability, which is not Taylor and Brown's criterion of the ability to care for and about others. The nearest pooled test of that criterion is Dufner's informant-rated communion, and its sign depends on which content domain the self-enhancement sits in.
misreadings: The 1988 paper is a literature review. Figures attributed to it belong to the studies it cites, and it reports no effect of its own. Taylor and Brown do not claim that illusion is necessary for mental health, that more illusion is better, or that illusions cure disease, and they say all three in print in 1994. The qualifier about moderate illusion belongs to that reply, not to the original paper, which speaks of overly positive and unrealistic beliefs without grading them. Depressive realism is often presented as the evidence the thesis rests on; Taylor and Brown say their argument does not depend on it, and entry 55 records that it did not survive replication. The finding is also flattened in both directions. Colvin and Block reported no data of their own, and their case is that the benefit is unproven and may be seriously wrong rather than that illusions damage mental health. Dufner's meta-analysis does not vindicate the whole formulation, because the personal half comes out positive while the interpersonal half splits by content. Robins and Beer add a timing qualification. Students who overrated their academic ability on entry showed falling self-esteem and well-being and growing disengagement over college, with no gain in grades or graduation rates.

sources.text: Taylor, S. E., & Brown, J. D. (1988). Illusion and well-being: A social psychological perspective on mental health. Psychological Bulletin, 103(2), 193-210. Read in full on 21 September 2026 from the authors' own laboratory copy of the published article at UCLA, the publisher's record being closed. The selection of criteria from Jahoda and from Jourard and Landsman, the summary conceding that the evidence is only suggestive, and the cancer passages were all checked there.

Colvin, C. R., & Block, J. (1994). Do positive illusions foster mental health? An examination of the Taylor and Brown formulation. Psychological Bulletin, 116(1), 3-20. Read in full on 21 September 2026 from an open teaching copy of the published article at Wabash College. ResearchGate answers its own copy with a bot challenge, not a paywall, and no index lists the paper as open. The scan carries no text layer and was read by optical character recognition, page by page. An earlier note on this entry called the paper paywalled and unread, which was wrong.

Read in full on 21 September 2026 from the authors' own laboratory copy of the published article at UCLA. The three narrowings and the disclaimer about depressive realism were checked there.
